title: Number of Provinces
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated full-matrix merging scans versus DFS/BFS from each unvisited city.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an n by n matrix isConnected, where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly connected, return the number of provinces (a province is a group of directly or indirectly connected cities, not connected to any other group).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","isConnected adjacency matrix"],["Output","Number of connected components (provinces)"],["Goal","For every unvisited city, run DFS/BFS to mark its entire connected group visited, counting how many such searches start"],["Constraints","Up to 200 cities"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Count groups of directly or indirectly connected items\"","A classic connected-components counting problem, solvable via DFS/BFS (or Union-Find), counting how many separate searches are needed to cover the whole graph"]]}

blocks.text: This is exactly a connected-components counting problem: treat isConnected as an adjacency matrix representing a graph, and count how many separate connected components exist. Each time a city is found unvisited, it must belong to a NEW province, so a search from it marks its entire group visited, and the count increments.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Isolated Social Circles From a Direct-Friendship Chart
blocks.text: Picture a chart showing which people are direct friends. Counting the number of separate, isolated friend circles (where everyone in a circle is connected to everyone else, directly or through mutual friends, but no circle connects to another) is exactly the same counting task.

blocks.caption: Each unvisited city starts a new province; DFS/BFS marks its entire connected group visited

blocks.text: Result: 2 (cities 0 and 1 form one province; city 2 forms its own).
Result: 3 (every city is its own separate province).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Any city not yet visited must belong to a province that has not yet been counted.

Observation 2: Running DFS (or BFS) from that city, following every direct connection recursively, correctly marks EVERY city in its entire connected group as visited, in one search.

Observation 3: Repeating this process (find an unvisited city, search its whole group, increment the count) for every city in the matrix correctly counts every distinct province exactly once.
This leads to iterating over every city, running DFS/BFS from each still-unvisited one, and counting how many such searches are started.
Conceptually, repeatedly scan the entire matrix, merging any newly discovered connections between groups, looping until a full scan produces no further merges.
Why the code is written this way

items: Repeatedly merging groups until no changes occur eventually reaches the correct grouping.
This costs many redundant full-matrix scans; a single DFS/BFS per unvisited city directly and efficiently discovers each entire province in one pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed) or worse, due to repeated full scans and merges.
Space: O(n) for the group array.
Limitation: a single DFS/BFS from every still-unvisited city directly discovers each province in one pass, without repeated scanning.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain a visited array, initially all false. For each city from 0 to n-1, if it is not yet visited, this must be a NEW province: increment the province count, then run DFS (or BFS) from this city, marking every reachable city (via direct connections in isConnected) as visited. After processing every city this way, the final count is the number of provinces.
Iterate over every city, running DFS/BFS from each still-unvisited one, counting how many searches are started.

blocks.content: {"headers":["City","Visited?","Action"],"rows":[["0","no","new province, DFS marks 0 and 1 visited, count=1"],["1","yes (already marked)","skip"],["2","no","new province, DFS marks just 2 visited, count=2"]]}

blocks.text: Since a DFS (or BFS) from any city correctly visits every city reachable from it via direct or indirect connections (its entire connected component), starting a fresh search only when an UNVISITED city is encountered correctly guarantees each distinct province is discovered exactly once, and the running count of such fresh searches exactly equals the number of provinces.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the adjacency matrix itself requires examining all n squared entries across all searches combined.
Space: O(n) for the visited array and recursion depth.

blocks.text: Number of Provinces is the foundational connected-components counting problem, directly applicable to any adjacency-matrix or adjacency-list graph.

items: Forgetting that isConnected[i][i] is always 1 (a city is trivially connected to itself), though this does not affect correctness since it is handled naturally by the visited check.
Re-running DFS from an already-visited city, wastefully rediscovering the same province multiple times.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "count connected components via DFS/BFS from each unvisited node" connects this problem immediately to a very standard graph technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "count groups of directly or indirectly connected items", think: connected-components counting via DFS, BFS, or Union-Find.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The repeated-scanning brute force costs O(n cubed) or worse; the DFS/BFS-per-unvisited-city approach costs O(n squared), the standard efficient solution.

items: Core Idea: every unvisited city starts a new province; DFS/BFS marks its entire connected group visited.
Time: O(n cubed) or worse for the brute force, O(n squared) for the DFS/BFS approach.
Most Important Observation: a fresh search should only start from a genuinely unvisited node.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy to medium graph connectivity problem.
One line memory trick: one search per unvisited node, count the searches.
